newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-UNITED SHELL-SHOCKED AFTER HISTORIC HOME DEFEAT.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-UNITED SHELL-SHOCKED AFTER HISTORIC HOME DEFEAT.

text.p: Manchester United's route-plan to the 1997 European Cup still lay open on the table on Thursday, but their proud 40-year record of continental success on English soil lay in tatters.

A single goal from Fenerbahce's Elvir Bolic in Wednesday's Group C Champions' League clash at Old Trafford put paid to a record kindled by the "Busby Babes" in the 1950s, strengthened by the United side that won Europe's premier trophy in 1968, and carried forward to the 1990s by Alex Ferguson's men.
Before Wednesday, United had gone 56 home matches in European competition without defeat, stretching back to a 10-0 rout of Anderlecht in the autumn of 1956.
AC Milan, Juventus, Benfica and Barcelona had all failed to leave Old Trafford with a victory. Few would have bet on the Turkish champions becoming the first side to do so.

United, who would have qualified for the quarter-finals if they had beaten Fenerbahce, now need four points from their remaining two matches -- against a rampant Juventus here and against Rapid Vienna in Austria -- to be sure of a place in the last eight.
Ferguson had hoped to put Europe to the back of his mind for a few months in which he could have rectified his side's embarrassing recent premier league form. That hope is gone.
United were disjointed throughout Wednesday's match, even though they rightly claimed afterwards they did not deserve to lose to an uninspiring Fenerbahce.

They home side failed to create a single real goal-scoring chance in the first half, and captain Eric Cantona, who has said publically he is bewildered and disappointed with his recent poor form, again played dismally.
His volley half-way through the first period summed up the home side's night.
Midfielder Nicky Butt hoisted the ball over the Fenerbahce defence, and Cantona, with all the time in the world, watched it drop and then skewed his right-foot shot well wide of the Turkish goal.

The Frenchman, who three seasons ago salvaged United's European home record with a late equaliser against Galatasaray in the European Cup, never looked likely of repeating the feat against Wednesday's visitors from Istanbul.
He hurried from Old Trafford just 20 minutes after the final whistle, surrounded by minders and declining to comment on the match.
The man who single-handedly guided the English league title towards Old Trafford last season with a series of crucial goals in March and April has seldom looked more out of sorts.
He cut a lone figure in United's front line on Wednesday, receiving minimal support from Karel Poborsky and Jordi Cruyff on the flanks.
But in truth, the United side as a whole was ineffectual, and Ferguson, the premier league's longest serving manager, has work to do if his side are to prosper this season.

Fenerbahce's vocal supporters entertained themselves by taunting the Stretford End with chants of Newcastle and Southampton -- the two sides which between them put 11 goals past United in the last fortnight -- and dignity on the domestic front must be Ferguson's short-term priority.

"It's an ironic life," he reflected afterwards. "You prepare to celebrate 10 years at a club and instead find yourself suffering the first home defeat in Europe. I had hoped it wouldn't happen during my time here."
